section.title: Life after the next promotion stops being the goal
section.deck: Philip Su examines career limits, the emotional cost of stepping down, and the need for meaning beyond status and financial security.

blocks.question: What did you think when you reached distinguished engineer—did you want another promotion?
answer: Early in his career, Su assumed that promotions would continue every few years and did not consider an eventual end. By level seven, he recognized that higher roles require more scope and that the business must actually need that scope. An organization might limit partner-level positions for budgetary and organizational reasons, irrespective of an individual’s ambition.

When Facebook first introduced level nine, the initial promotees seemed extraordinarily accomplished and universally recognized. He did not consider going further realistic. His recollection challenges the idea that every promotion simply starts another predictable step upward: roles narrow, opportunity matters, and people encounter limits.

blocks.question: What kept you growing through staff and beyond?
answer: For much of his Microsoft career, levels provided a substitute for the grades and tests he had enjoyed at school. Professional work offered few clear numerical indicators, so promotion felt like an achievement score. He actively pursued that score into his early thirties.

Beyond level seven, he became unsure whether he would enjoy the changing work or meet its expectations. His later promotions to eight and nine were consequences of work he found interesting, rather than explicit targets. Facebook was then small and mission-focused; he says he did not even know levels existed there until his manager told him he had been promoted.

blocks.question: What changed your view of promotion?
answer: The reward became less uncomplicated. A promotion brought expectations he was no longer certain he could fulfill. Staying at a level where he already enjoyed the work began to feel comfortable, and he recognized that it might be his final level.

He recalls immediately asking how to reach eight after a mentor promoted him to seven. The mentor asked whether they could spend one meeting celebrating. Years later, Su realized that this respected, more experienced mentor was himself at the same level. He now sees his earlier response as insufficiently humble: doing excellent work at an existing level is already a substantial accomplishment.

followups.question: What calmed the intense desire for more?
answer: He thinks age may contribute, while explicitly valuing young people’s ambition. A more concrete factor was the changing job. Up to about IC6, the work often felt like a larger version of coding, refactoring, and longer-term engineering projects.

For a generalist beyond that point, advancement increasingly means setting team direction, judging whether a product is worth building, and resolving conflicts between organizations. More meetings come with the work on either the IC or management path. He became less enthusiastic about those future changes. He acknowledges rare engineers whose exceptional coding ability supports another path.

blocks.question: Before seeking a demotion, did you ever ask not to be promoted beyond IC7?
answer: Not when moving from seven to eight: that promotion surprised him, and the smaller Facebook of that period still involved relatively little organizational overhead. Later, the Seattle office alone had grown from a handful of desks to more than two thousand people. Senior roles in a much larger organization contained more coordination and less direct technical work.

He distinguishes enjoyable people work—welcoming colleagues and creating collaborations—from politics, unhappy colleagues, and constructive feedback. He felt effective leading Facebook London but much less effective at some of the latter responsibilities. Even a senior IC without direct reports is expected to improve people around them, so opting out of management does not remove interpersonal demands.

followups.question: How did moving from IC9 to IC7 feel?
answer: It was difficult despite choosing it. Rising had felt like progress; being at the top mixed remarkable opportunities with exhausting expectations. He felt a continuing spotlight on whether the company was receiving value from a highly paid senior employee.

Watching people formerly below his level rise above him brought wistfulness rather than a wish to limit their success. He remembered being capable of that work and wondered whether he could do it again. His Beowulf analogy expresses the desire to deliver one last great performance, while accepting that this may no longer be right for him.

blocks.question: What changed that made the higher level harder to sustain?
answer: His environment changed. In a small company, his generalist range was useful: for Facebook video calling, he wrote code, negotiated partner contracts, dealt with testing arrangements, and spoke to the press. A large company assigns those tasks to specialized functions. He thinks senior domain experts fit that setting better, while his own strengths became less relevant.

One later team spent an entire half fixing bugs in an internal tool. He was willing to help, but it was not work in which he felt especially distinguished. Meanwhile, he tired of the pressure to meet senior expectations. Earlier, being the weakest person on a team could feel exciting because he was catching up; later it felt like a recurring risk rather than a desirable challenge.

followups.question: Was that pressure mostly impostor syndrome, given your promotions?
answer: He allows that some may have been, but considers much of it an honest assessment of fit. At IC4 he could imagine doing many IC5 jobs with time. At IC7 he could see peers doing work he did not believe he could do. Higher-level business roles also become more specific: the organization needs a particular combination of technical and other strengths, and his own shape did not match many of them.

blocks.question: Why did you work extreme hours after you stopped pursuing promotions?
answer: Shipping the first Facebook video-calling version brought a strong sense of mission. During six weeks in Menlo Park, he describes moving almost directly between work and sleep and losing about ten pounds. He was not seeking a level; he enjoyed seeing users benefit from fixes and believed easier video calling would matter.

The tiny team created a sense of responsibility to colleagues who were working equally hard. Direct contact with user problems and a meaningful product supplied motivation that the promotion score had previously supplied. His recollection explains his choice; it is not presented as a prescription for everyone’s hours.

blocks.question: Looking back, was working so hard worth it?
answer: Su understands why successful, wealthy people telling younger people to slow down can sound unpersuasive. Some tradeoffs become clearer only after living them. For his personality, very senior roles with broad people-oriented pressure became a poor long-term fit.

He also recognizes what the career bought him: enough savings to spend two years building his own software. He does not reject the earlier work outright. His regret is that he pushed without understanding the exchange he was making. Greater awareness could have connected present effort to future freedom and made competing priorities explicit.

blocks.question: Is advice useless if people only understand it after experience?
answer: He distinguishes ignoring advice from never having heard it. Advice provides a reference point: when the consequence arrives, someone can recognize it and act sooner. It can also cause a person to pause at a later decision even if they do not follow it immediately.

His small example is buying an expensive, highly recommended pen once he felt financially secure. It was slippery and rolled away; he preferred a cheap familiar pen. The disappointment made advice about consumption and happiness concrete. He uses the story to show delayed understanding, not to claim every expensive purchase disappoints.

blocks.question: After financial security, what provides meaning outside the earnings treadmill?
answer: He distinguishes personalities that remain content with prolonged leisure from his own need for goals. A week on a beach feels wonderful; an extended stay starts to feel purposeless. His analogy of an animal endlessly triggering pleasure expresses why pleasure alone does not constitute fulfillment for him.

He imagines that the saving phase of financial independence could be more satisfying than retirement for someone like him: it gives a measurable goal and repeated evidence of progress. He says he never adopted the movement himself. Periods without work exposed his difficulty answering what he should do next. This is self-description, not a judgment that others’ retirement preferences are wrong.

blocks.question: Would you have been happier with slower promotions spread across your whole career?
answer: He initially thinks spreading the rewards out might have helped, then acknowledges the dilemma. Six promotions over a forty-two-year career would imply seven years per step, which he would have found painfully slow at the beginning. Faster early growth leaves very long intervals later, or decades with no promotion.

The arithmetic is illustrative rather than a proposed career plan. It reveals that promotion cannot remain the sole source of motivation for an entire career. He also wonders whether a late reward has the same appeal as an earlier one, using a sports-car purchase as an analogy. He remains torn rather than endorsing deliberate slow advancement.

blocks.question: Have you found meaning without an immediate career goal?
answer: For him, regular social contact is essential. Work supplies a recurring shared place and schedule. After quitting Facebook for six months, he expected coffee with former colleagues to fill that gap, but they were busy working.

His best period between jobs came when two former colleagues were also available. They skied on weekdays and spent time together regularly. He uses an imaginative comparison with leisure-class social life to express the difference: free time is more satisfying when others can share it. Whether employed or not, he now considers a reliable social setting central to happiness.

blocks.question: Which book helped you think about life and career choices?
answer: He recommends Four Thousand Weeks because viewing a life as a finite number of weeks made time more precious and clarified his need to examine values. The recommendation is his account of what helped him, with no claim that it answers every reader’s situation.

followups.question: What practical question did it help you ask?
answer: Visualize your largest current goal, then imagine you have achieved it and ask what happens the next day. A satisfying answer suggests something durable beyond the goal itself. Su did not have that answer and compares the resulting difficulty to athletes who reach the peak without building another identity or set of skills. He encourages planning for the day after success.

blocks.question: If you could begin again, what would you change?
answer: He would change periods when he made himself maximally available to the employer and minimally available to friends and family. Some work he justified as helping the family also meant he was rarely present with them.

Interestingly, he does not single out the intense video-calling launch as the main regret. His family moved to California with him, and he remembers that arrangement as making the period more acceptable even with very little daily time together. Other periods involved routine absence without that shared context.

followups.question: Would prioritizing family have reduced your career success?
answer: Possibly, and he considers the exchange worthwhile. He does not know the counterfactual: breaks can improve performance when fatigue creates errors, so shorter hours might sometimes have helped him professionally.

He also rejects an unconditional promise that forty hours produces the same results as longer work. All else equal, he expects sustained additional effort to affect results and rewards. His conclusion is therefore candid about costs: he suspects greater family availability could have affected his career, and would still accept that tradeoff.

blocks.title: What changed as Su’s career and company grew
rows: Promotion supplied a clear achievement score.
Interesting work, fit, and acceptable expectations mattered more.
A small company rewarded broad generalist contributions.
A large company separated those tasks into specialist roles.
More scope could resemble larger coding projects.
Greater scope involved product judgment and organizational influence.
Financial security and a senior level required a new answer to what comes next.

coverage.reason: Read every compact-reading chunk in order; preserved substantive exchanges and recorded repetitive trailer and housekeeping omissions.

editorial.notes: All four chunks read. Keeps the distinction between ability, environment fit, organizational opportunity, and personal preference. Leisure and work-hour assessments remain personality-dependent. Career and family counterfactuals stay uncertain; the illustrative promotion arithmetic is not a universal ladder.
